description:
I’m Glory Abayomi, a Remote Sensing and GIS student My interests are satellite radar, ground deformation and natural hazards, and my skills are InSAR processing, GIS and geospatial Python.

For “Dancing with the SARs” I’m building a web app that uses NISAR radar to monitor unstable slopes above the Lhende Khola in Rasuwa, Nepal, where an avalanche caused a flood in August 2026.

I’d welcome teammates with skills in web design and front-end development, science communication or video.
summary: On 26 August 2026 a rock-ice avalanche from Langtang Lirung entered the Lhende Khola and sent a flood down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers in Rasuwa, Nepal. We built Rasuwa Monitor, a near-real-time web application that tracks surface deformation on the slopes around the source using NISAR L-band SAR. Starting from Level-1 Range-Doppler Single Look Complex (RSLC) data, our pipeline forms 12-day repeat-pass differential interferograms on ascending track 98 and descending track 48 with ISCE3, including coregistration, phase unwrapping, ionospheric phase correction and geocoding. Unwrapped phase is converted to line-of-sight (LOS) displacement, and the ascending and descending LOS measurements are decomposed into vertical and east-west horizontal components. Ten sequential interferometric pairs from June to November 2026 give a cumulative displacement time series, with coherence used to mask unreliable pixels. It addresses the challenge by taking NISAR from SLC to an interpretable deformation product that a non-specialist can read. It matters because the same valley can fail again, and communities downstream have little warning.
details:
What it does. Rasuwa Monitor is a near-real-time web application for monitoring slope deformation above the Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi in Rasuwa, Nepal, the site of the 26 August 2026 Langtang Lirung rock-ice avalanche. It covers ten 12-day repeat-pass periods from 20 June to 11 November 2026 over a 30 by 25 km area. For each period it maps line-of-sight (LOS) displacement from the ascending and descending orbits and, where both are coherent, decomposes them into vertical and east-west displacement. A simple view classifies each pixel as uplift, subsidence or within the noise level of that pair; a detailed view shows the continuous displacement scale. Clicking a pixel gives its displacement, a cumulative displacement time series from the first acquisition with a linear fit and an uncertainty band, and a marker for the avalanche date. Up to five points can be pinned and compared, for example on both banks of the river. An interferogram network shows which acquisitions were paired and the mean coherence of each pair.

How it works. I wrote a single Python script that searches the Alaska Satellite Facility archive for NISAR L-band L1 RSLC (single look complex) scenes, downloads them, crops them to the area of interest, and runs JPL’s ISCE3 InSAR workflow on OpenSARlab: coregistration, interferogram formation, phase unwrapping, ionospheric correction and geocoding. The script then converts unwrapped phase to LOS displacement in millimetres, removes the elevation-dependent (stratified) tropospheric delay, decomposes the ascending and descending LOS displacement into vertical and east-west components, estimates the noise level of each pair, flags deformation above that level, and uploads the products to Amazon S3, where a React and Leaflet web app reads them. I automated the script for near-real-time monitoring: it queries the ASF archive on a schedule and, as soon as a new 12-day NISAR acquisition is available on both orbits, processes it and publishes the updated deformation products to the web app.

Benefit and impact. Local authorities, researchers and the public can see which slopes above the river are deforming, and how reliable each measurement is, without processing SAR data themselves. The same pipeline can be applied to any other site by changing four settings.

What I considered. Displacement is relative: each pair is referenced to the scene median, not to a GNSS-tied stable point. Snow cover causes temporal decorrelation, and steep terrain causes layover and shadow; these low-coherence areas are masked and shown in grey. The avalanche marker does not prove that the event caused any measured displacement. This is a monitoring prototype, not a validated early-warning system.

Tools. Python, ISCE3, GDAL, asf_search, OpenSARlab, Amazon S3, JavaScript, React, Vite, Leaflet, geotiff.js.

Use of AI. I used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant to write the code. I chose the problem, the site and the method, ran all the processing, set up the hosting, and reviewed the results. The voice-over and background music in the demo video are AI-generated. No AI-generated images or video are used; every map and value comes from NISAR data
